title: Quiz: Political Economy Review: Capital and Surplus Value Concepts

questions.question: What is the primary difference between ordinary money and capital in their movement purpose?
questions.explanation: Ordinary money circulates to facilitate exchange (H T H), but capital circulates to generate surplus value (T H T').

answers.text: Both ordinary money and capital move according to the same circulation formula H T H.
Ordinary money creates surplus value by exploiting labor, unlike capital, which is only a medium of exchange.
Ordinary money serves as a medium of circulation following the formula H T H, while capital moves according to the formula T H T'.
Capital serves as a medium of circulation and follows the formula H T H, while ordinary money produces surplus value.

questions.question: Why are capital divided into constant capital and variable capital?
questions.explanation: Constant capital (means of production) is necessary for production but doesn't create surplus value; variable capital (labor power) is the source of surplus value.

answers.text: Because constant capital creates surplus value and variable capital does not.
Because constant capital is money only, and variable capital is machinery only.
Because they have different roles: constant capital is necessary for production, while variable capital creates surplus value.
Because constant capital changes form during circulation and variable capital remains fixed.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes circulating capital?
questions.explanation: Circulating capital includes variable capital (wages) and raw materials that are fully consumed in production cycles.

answers.text: Circulating capital includes all means of production and fixed capital.
Circulating capital consists only of fixed machinery and equipment.
Circulating capital is only money capital and does not include labor wages.
Circulating capital includes wages, raw materials, and variable capital components involved in production.

questions.question: What effect does technological progress have on capital composition and unemployment?
questions.explanation: Advancement in technology raises constant capital's share relative to variable capital, reducing labor demand and increasing unemployment.

answers.text: Technological progress reduces the technical composition of capital and increases employment.
Technological progress increases the technical composition of capital, reduces variable capital, and leads to higher unemployment.
Technological progress increases variable capital and has no effect on unemployment.
Technological progress decreases fixed capital and lowers unemployment.

questions.question: Why is labor power considered a special commodity?
questions.explanation: Labor power is unique as it produces value exceeding its own, due to its dual nature and social conditions embedded in its value.

answers.text: Because its value is always equal to the wages paid and cannot create surplus value.
Because it is identical to all other commodities and has a fixed use value only.
Because when used, it creates new value greater than its own, including factors like historical and mental elements.
Because labor power has no exchange value and is not a commodity in capitalist production.

questions.question: How is surplus value produced in capitalist production?
questions.explanation: Surplus value arises because workers work beyond the time necessary to reproduce their wages, producing unpaid labor.

answers.text: By having equal amounts of necessary and surplus labor time.
By ensuring the time of surplus labor is greater than the time of necessary labor in the working day.
By reducing working hours below the necessary labor time to create surplus.
By increasing the wages paid to workers above their labor value.

questions.question: What is the relationship between labor productivity and the value of a commodity unit?
questions.explanation: Higher productivity reduces socially necessary labor time per unit, lowering its value accordingly.

answers.text: They are directly proportional; as productivity increases, value per unit increases.
They are inversely proportional; as productivity increases, the value per unit decreases.
There is no connection between labor productivity and commodity value.
Labor productivity affects only total output but not the value of individual units.

questions.question: Which statement best describes fixed capital depreciation?
questions.explanation: Fixed capital depreciates both physically (wear) and in value during production use.

answers.text: Fixed capital does not depreciate as it retains full value indefinitely.
It only includes physical wear and tear, not value loss.
It includes both physical wear and value depreciation through use.
It happens only when fixed capital is sold or replaced.

questions.question: Why is the right to use land considered a special commodity?
questions.explanation: Land use rights have a use and exchange value but do not embody labor-created value, making them special commodities.

answers.text: Because it is produced by human labor and has exchange value like ordinary commodities.
Because it can be consumed and reproduced like consumer goods.
Because it loses value when used and must be replaced frequently.
Because it grants exploitation of land with use value and price but lacks value created by labor.

questions.question: What happens to capital accumulation under conditions of increasing production concentration?
questions.explanation: Accumulation and concentration of capital both lead to growth in the size of individual capital and overall social capital.

answers.text: Accumulation reduces scale while concentration has no effect.
Neither accumulation nor concentration affects capital scale.
Both accumulation and concentration increase the scale of individual and social capital.
Concentration increases scale but accumulation reduces it.
